runs.text: argumenta, ou fala ſem ordem, & ſem meto

lines.note: This completes the proverb Figacuxa ronguini maqezu on Gallica f190: the ill-informed disputant argues without order or method. The next row completes metodo; no additional hyphen is supplied here.

runs.text: do de letras. i, ſem logica, não ha ficar vẽcido

lines.note: Sem logica explains the lack of scholarly method: such a disputant will not be defeated on those terms. The explanatory i belongs to the Portuguese passage; preserve the nasal abbreviation in vẽcido.

Higakushi is a sunshade, explained as hi no ooi, a covering against the sun. The historical vouoi spelling is retained rather than replaced with a modernized romanization; the Portuguese antepairo likewise describes a screen or shelter.

runs.text: ra o ſol como o que fazem os Iapoẽs ſobre as ſe

lines.note: The gloss gives Japanese examples of these sunshades above graves. Se continues as sepulturas on the next physical row; the absence of a hyphen does not imply a separate word.

runs.text: pulturas dos mortos, ou às portas das boticas,

lines.note: The second location is the doorway of a botica, a shop here, not necessarily a pharmacy. Preserve the printed grave accent in às.
Tendas supplies another word for shops or stalls, completing the sunshade examples rather than starting a new Japanese entry.

runs.text: Erro na vista vendo hũa couſa por

lines.note: Higame denotes mistaken sight: taking one thing for another. The enlarged crop supports hũa, not OCR hãa; the mark belongs over u.
Outra completes vendo hũa cousa por outra. This short continuation is a full-width line crop, not an independently magnified word image.

runs.text: Panela de poluora que ſe arremeſa

lines.note: The homophone higame here is a fire-pot, not defective vision: a pot of gunpowder that is thrown. Retain the locally printed arremeſa rather than silently doubling its s.
The pot is thrown alight to burn its target. This continuation establishes the incendiary sense of the preceding headword.
Higami, higamu, higǒda gives the inflection of higamu, to become or be crooked. The contracted past ending is historical morphology, not a reason to add a missing consonant to the abbreviated entry.
Kokoro no higǒda hito describes someone with a crooked heart. The adjective supplies a figurative moral application of the preceding verb; ru- continues as ruim below.
Ruim coração and peruerſa condição both describe a bad disposition. The scan supports u in peruerſa, the historical u/v spelling of modern perversa, not the OCR sequence perc-.

runs.text: Certos dias, em que fazem os gentios

lines.note: Higan is the Buddhist seasonal observance. Gentios is the missionaries' term for non-Christians in this description; the scan restores its n, lost in OCR.

runs.text: na prima vera, & no Outono boas obras, &

lines.note: Spring and autumn identify the two seasonal higan periods. The printed prima vera is left separated, and boas obras describes the observances in the gloss's own vocabulary.

runs.text: rezão pera que lhe ſirua pera a outra vida, ou

lines.note: They pray for benefit in the next life, with an alternative beneficiary continuing below. Outra is both visible and required by outra vida; the OCR i was a misread t.
The alternative is benefit for their deceased relatives or associates. Defuntos, visible despite a weak u, completes the higan description; it is not defantos.

runs.text: Certa eſpecie de cereijeira q̃ flo-

lines.note: Higanzakura is a cherry tree flowering at higan. Cereijeira is the Portuguese tree name; the weak e after j was read as c by OCR. The printed flo- joins rece below: retain florece rather than modernizing it to floresce.

runs.text: rece na prima vera, naquelles dias do

lines.note: The flowering occurs in spring on those higan days. Figan is visibly roman within the italic Portuguese explanation and is an embedded Japanese term, not another headword.

runs.text: Paredes, ou cercas feitas com a caſcas

lines.note: Higaki denotes walls or fences made from bark. The apparently mismatched a caſcas is preserved as printed rather than grammatically repaired to as caſcas.

runs.text: ou cortiça de hũa aruore con o acipreste.

lines.note: The bark comes from a tree compared with a cypress. Hũa replaces the OCR haa. The printed comparison reads con o, although como o would be expected Portuguese; do not silently regularize that local sequence.

runs.text: Certa diuiſa pintada no veſtido, ou ex-

lines.note: This higaki is a decorative device, painted on clothing or impressed on swords. It is a separate sense from the physical fence, even if the motif may be related.
Expreßa completes the preceding ex- and describes the device on catanas. Catanas is visibly italic here; Japanese origin alone does not justify making it roman.
Higaki is also the name of a play, the sense identified by auto. The three identically spelled headwords have distinct glosses; they are not accidental duplicates.
Higara names a small bird. The gloss does not provide enough diagnostic detail for a species identification, so the comment does not extend the printed evidence into taxonomy.

runs.text: Olhos que tem algũa belida, ou carne-

lines.note: This higara instead concerns eyes with a white opacity or a fleshy growth. Belida and the following carnegão are Portuguese eye-condition vocabulary, not descriptions of the bird above.

runs.text: gão, ou homẽ q̃ olha com olhos desta maneira.

lines.note: Carnegão completes carne-; the term can also describe the person with such eyes. Preserve the nasal abbreviations in homẽ and q̃ rather than expanding them.
Higarame has the same eye-related meaning as the immediately preceding higara. Me supports the connection with eyes, but the printed entry itself simply says Idem.
Higasa is a sunshade or parasol. The long ſ in the Japanese headword remains distinct from f; the meaning matches the Portuguese protection against the sun.
Higashi means east. The historical xi corresponds to shi; the compact Portuguese gloss is complete on this row.
Higashimuki means facing east. The example begins Figaxi and continues muqini iru below; do not manufacture a new headword or insert a missing syllable at that physical break.

Higaxi muqini iru means to be facing east. The crop supports Estar, with the s/t group, rather than OCR Ettar; the change restores the Portuguese infinitive without modernizing the surrounding spelling.

runs.text: O ir, & tornar no meſmo dia.

lines.note: Higaeri means going and returning on the same day. The y in gayeri is part of the historical spelling and does not require a different lexical interpretation.
Higaeri ni suru expresses making a same-day trip. Idem refers back to the preceding definition, while the paragraph sign introduces the example.
Hige is a beard. Gui would represent gi, whereas the printed gue represents ge here; the headword and concise Portuguese gloss agree.
The separate hige sense is abasement or lowliness, not facial hair. Waga mi wo hige-suru is to humble oneself; the example's suru continues on the next row.
The faint final letter is read as u, giving hige-suru rather than OCR hige-sura. Humilharſe corroborates the Japanese verb meaning to humble oneself.
Higeko is a small basket. Canastrinha is another diminutive basket term; the printed n corrects OCR r without altering the retained spelling of Ceſtinho.
Higi is explained by hidǒ, unjust or unreasonable conduct. Gui denotes gi here, distinct from the gi spelling for the historical ji sound in the elbow entries in column 2.
Higyǒ is flying, paraphrased as tobi yuku. The faint i after F at the right edge completes Fi-, which joins guiǒ below; the caron is retained in the headword.

runs.text: O voar, ou diſcorrer com li-

lines.note: Figuiǒ jizai describes flying freely. Jizai is 自在; the Portuguese verb discorrer here concerns ranging or moving about, not necessarily delivering a discourse.
Ligeireza and liuremente complete the explanation of free, agile flight. The word split li-geireza belongs to the physical lineation only.

runs.text: Eſtes dias paſſados, ou ha poucos dias.

lines.note: Higoro here means these past days or a short time ago. Do not replace this attested temporal sense with only modern habitual or everyday usage.
Higotai names a red flower in this gloss; rosa should not be used to impose a modern botanical species. The row is visibly indented despite beginning an entry, so that layout is preserved.
The transferred sense is a girdle or belt with tassels. Cingidouro is one word, with a faint r rather than the OCR gap; Permet. abbreviates the figurative-use explanation.
Higoto and higoto ni both mean each day. The intervening l is the Latin alternative marker, not a Japanese syllable or part of the headword.

Higan is expanded as jihi no gan, the compassionate vow made by Amida. Initial Ii in Iifino is consonantal Ji, not an ordinary ii vowel sequence. The scan restores Voto and Amida; the object of the vow continues at the top of column 2.
This completes the vow in column 1: Amida vowed to save human beings. It is a cross-column continuation, not an unrelated introductory fragment.
Higuchi is the firearm's priming or ignition point, glossed with escorva. The historical u/v spelling Eſcorua is retained.

runs.text: Hũa eſpecie de cigarra que canta

lines.note: Higurashi names a kind of cicada. The following row supplies when it sings; the gloss is more specific than merely an insect name.

runs.text: nas tardes do estio, ou Outono.

lines.note: The cicada sings in summer or autumn afternoons. Estio is summer, not a mistaken form of a Japanese word, and its s/t typography is retained from the OCR reading.

runs.text: A tarde de pois do ſol posto.

lines.note: Higure is evening after sunset. Keep the printed de pois spacing rather than modernizing it to depois.
Hiji and hijigane denote the projecting part of a hinge. Historical gi gives the ji sound here; the gloss continues with the male/female distinction.
The receiving or female part is tsubo. Tçubo is roman within the Portuguese gloss; Figi starts the compound example completed below.
Figi tçubo is the hinge pair or assembly. This short physical continuation must remain separate in Level 1, even though the Japanese phrase spans two rows.
Hijigane repeats the male hinge-part sense explicitly. This is a legitimate independent headword after the compound example, not a duplicated continuation.
Hiji is the elbow. Hiji wo haru, to spread or brace the elbows, begins an example whose Portuguese description continues with hands on the hips.

runs.text: mãos nas ilhargas arcando os braços. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: The hands rest on the flanks or hips with the arms bent outward. Nas, visible in the crop, replaces OCR nae; Itẽ introduces the figurative extension below.
The same posture expresses pride or swagger. Preserve historical oufano; the next Japanese phrase begins a new example with the same object, hiji wo.
Hiji wo kudaku is glossed as working very hard. Its literal elbow-breaking wording is idiomatic here, not a bodily injury contradicting the Portuguese.
Hiji wo maguru means bending the arm. Keep maguru as the printed historical verb form rather than substituting modern mageru; the following example splits maguete across rows.
Hiji wo maguete makura ni suru describes bending the elbow and using it as a pillow. The scan and the te-form support guete, not OCR gucte; the kana failure on gucte was a useful diagnostic.
Cotouelo completes co- and the explanation of sleeping on one's elbow. The row contains only this Portuguese continuation.
Hijigasa ame, marked poetic by italic P., is explained as niwaka na ame, a sudden shower. The elbow-as-umbrella image is explained below; the Latin i is not a Japanese syllable.

runs.text: ua repentina que paſſa logo em quanto ſe hum

lines.note: The shower passes quickly while someone shields themselves. The visible long-s group supports paſſa, not OCR paſca; this is also the verb required by the Portuguese sentence.

runs.text: cobre com o braço, ou manga do braço.

lines.note: One shelters under an arm or sleeve, explaining the poetic compound hijigasa. This description is an interpretation supplied by the dictionary itself, not a modern speculative etymology.
Hijitsubo denotes the door-hinge assembly. The entry explicitly includes both components, in contrast with hijigane above.
Femea completes the male-and-female pair in the preceding hinge definition. Its short length does not make it furniture or a detached headword.
Hijiri, hijiru, hijitta is a verb for twisting or being crooked, distinct from the later noun Fijiri, holy person. Gi and ji must not be merged merely because their modern reflexes can sound alike.
Yugami hijitta ki ja means that it is a bent, twisted piece of wood. The final X. marks regional usage; the predicate qigia is ki plus ja, not an unidentified longer noun.

Hijǔ is explained as hi no uchi, during the day. The decorated initial is E in Entre, not OCR L. Enlargement confirms the marked u, and the post-reading NINJAL comparison independently supports Figiǔ.

Fijde gives hiide, followed by the abbreviated forms hiizzuru and hiideta: plants emerging or sprouting. Do not replace the printed jd sequence with a modern spelling; trigo continues across the line break. NINJAL likewise identifies this historical verb rather than treating jd as an OCR error.
Wheat completes the literal examples. Item, Permet. introduces a figurative application of emerging, explained by começar a on this row.

runs.text: valer, & dar de ſi luz no mundo não a tendo

lines.note: The figurative sense is beginning to have worth or distinction and shine in the world. Valer is visible and meaningful here; OCR vuler obscured the Portuguese verb.
Dantes completes the contrast with a previous lack of distinction. The isolated S. is a usage label and remains italic with the surrounding gloss.
Fiina names the leafy plant glossed as bredos, with X. marking the regional form. The scan contains the n missed by OCR; the Cami form follows below.
Hiuna is the corresponding Cami plant name. Keep the u diacritic as a graphic feature of the printed form rather than deriving its shape from modern hiyuna.

runs.text: O fazer as partes dalguem, ou procu-

lines.note: Hiiki is acting in someone's interest or taking their part. Here ij represents the long i sequence; the meaning corroborates the headword without altering its spelling.
Hito no hiiki wo suru exemplifies supporting someone. Procurar por elle continues the Portuguese gloss; its first syllables are on the preceding row.
Hiiragi is a woodland tree. The lexical identification is consistent with holly-like hiiragi, but the Portuguese gives only the broad tree description.
The verb hiiragu concerns a wound burning or throbbing, not the tree in the preceding entry. The inflectional abbreviations must be read with the verb's stem, not as independent words.

runs.text: que madura, &c. No Cami ſe diz, fijraqu.

lines.note: The wound is ripening or coming to a head. The regional alternative fijraqu has a visible r, not OCR c; both Cami and fijraqu are printed italic here despite being Japanese words.

runs.text: Borboleta que ſae do bicho da ſeda.

lines.note: Hiiru names the moth emerging from the silkworm. The scan restores the weak r in the headword and the damaged Portuguese borboleta and bicho; the gloss identifies an insect, not an ordinary verb ending in -iru.
Hiji means a secret matter, explained as kakusu koto, something concealed. This is distinct from figi, elbow, whose g is a different printed character.
This homophone names a meal of Buddhist clergy. Cea is an older spelling of Portuguese ceia and begins with a capital C in the scan; no additional i is supplied.

Hijin combines the organs identified as hi no zǒ and jin no zǒ. Preserve the dictionary's stomach-and-kidneys gloss rather than replacing its historical anatomical identification with a modern one for 脾.
Hijini is death from hunger, here phrased as allowing oneself to starve. Fi- continues into jiniſuru below; the split must not make the example a different Japanese word.
Together with Fi- above, this reads fijiniſuru, to die of hunger. The beginning of this row is not a standalone jini headword.
Hijiki is described as a kind of marine growth or seaweed. Limos do mar provides the expected sense; qi represents ki, not a q followed by an omitted Portuguese-style u.
Hijiri is illustrated by Koya-hijiri, itinerant Buddhist religious figures. Preserve qe as printed rather than inserting u solely to produce the more familiar Portuguese que.

runs.text: dão peregrinando com huns ceſtos, ou modo

lines.note: They travel on pilgrimage with baskets, or things like baskets. The weak u in huns and o in modo are read with the intact surrounding letters and phrase, rather than preserving OCR's unmotivated gap in modo.

runs.text: de canaſtras às costas. ¶ Item, Fijiri

lines.note: The baskets are carried on their backs: costas, not OCR coſtes. Fijiri introducing the next sense is visibly italic within this row, so its Japanese status does not automatically change its typeface.

runs.text: Bonzos principaes que tem algũa dignidade

lines.note: Hijiri can also designate leading clergy holding some rank. The crop supports principaes and algũa; neither OCR trincipaes nor algãa expresses the visible letter sequence.
The term can also include ordinary clergy. This completes the body; the Fijiri at the lower right is a catchword, not another definition on this page.
